8: Iteration 4 goes from variant to mechanism to medicine using only its own evidence, in three stages, each a case-agnostic tool with a provenance manifest. (1) Mechanism from five instruments that share no data: open variant-effect models run under one contract (AlphaMissense, ESM1b, REVEL place the missense allele in their top 0.47-2.59 %; GPN-MSA ranks the pair 508th of 54,865); a Boltz-2 fold of wild-type vs mutant BubR1 (inconclusive); a ThermoMPNN stability atlas of all 19,950 BubR1 substitutions, calibrated on published MVA allele classes before the child's allele was placed (the missense is at the 87th percentile, predicted destabilising); a phenotype twin that scores the child's 8 HPO terms against all 76,699 MGI mouse genotypes (a Bub1b hypomorph in the top 1.0-1.4 %, about 10x chance); and a gene ranking on the HPO terms (BUB1B 14th of 5,267). Reading: loss of function, too little stable BubR1. (2) Candidates from four generators whose rules were committed before any join: a PrimeKG walk from the MVA disease node (top 50 labelled drugs); the twin's published rescues (approved analogues: dasatinib, niacin); a screen-wide sweep of 613 approved drugs in PRISM for rhabdomyosarcoma- and aneuploidy-selective killing (top 0.5 % per contrast); and LINCS signature reversal of the BUB1B CRISPR-knockout signature in two engines (SigCom LINCS, iLINCS). Their agreement was tested against a 10,000-draw permutation null. (3) Three checks that can filter but never propose: direction (checkpoint-kinase inhibitors fail, measured in PRISM as less effective in aneuploid lines; spindle poisons a caution); the child's own safety from two sources side by side (PharmCAT/CPIC on the child's VCF, and OnSIDES/FAERS label effects matched to the child's HPO terms); and a contrary screen result. Result: 62 drugs; the generators agree on one, dasatinib, which is what chance gives (p 0.263); it passes every check. Every claim was registered before its test, and the refuted and uninterpretable ones are reported as such. The chain was re-run on a second disease (Bloom syndrome) by configuration.
9: Automated. Every candidate list comes from a generator rule written and committed before any join: a knowledge-graph walk (PrimeKG), a cross-species phenotype match over MGI with its published interventions, a screen-wide statistical sweep over PRISM, and connectivity queries to SigCom LINCS and iLINCS. The checks are automated too (PharmCAT, CPIC API, OnSIDES, openFDA FAERS). No LLM ranked or selected drugs.
10: Manual work is limited and recorded. (a) The phenotype twin's intervention table (12 rows) was read from paper abstracts, each with a verified PMID, and marks whether each rescue supports a direction. (b) The published MVA allele classes used to calibrate the stability atlas (8 alleles) were labelled from full texts with verbatim evidence (entry 149). (c) The mapping from the child's HPO terms to MedDRA adverse-effect terms is a hand-built, inspectable table (hpo_to_adverse_terms.tsv). (d) The report's wording and the direction table were written by hand from the entries. No candidate was added or removed by hand.
11: Publicly available sources only. No proprietary data source was used.
12: PrimeKG (Harvard Dataverse, CC0; DrugBank-derived drug nodes); openFDA drug labels and FAERS (public domain); MGI genotype-phenotype reports and the MP ontology, HPO and phenotype.hpoa, the Mouse-Human Mapping Initiative SSSOM (CC BY 4.0); PRISM Repurposing 24Q2 and 20Q2, DepMap 24Q4 model and omics signatures (CC BY 4.0, figshare mirrors, sha256 recorded); LINCS L1000 via SigCom LINCS and iLINCS; ChEMBL (max phase); the Drug Repurposing Hub mechanism labels shipped with PRISM; PharmCAT 3.4.0 with its bundled CPIC/DPWG/FDA annotations; the CPIC API; OnSIDES v3.1.1 (CC BY 4.0); AlphaFold DB (BubR1 model), UniProt, InterPro, CDD; ThermoMPNN (MIT); Boltz-2; AlphaMissense, ESM1b, REVEL, GPN-MSA, Evo 2, NT-v2, ESM-C score tables or models; PubMed (every cited PMID resolved via NCBI E-utilities).
14: Loss of function, hypomorphic, of a compound heterozygote confirmed by the challenge's answer key: one stop_gained allele (no full-length protein) and one missense allele in BUB1B. The missense was read by five independent instruments: variant-effect models place it in their top 0.47-2.59 % and GPN-MSA ranks the pair at the 0.93rd percentile; a ThermoMPNN stability atlas puts it at the 87th percentile of all 19,950 possible substitutions, buried in the pseudokinase domain (predicted destabilising; the predictor could not separate published allele classes at n = 8, so the class is a prediction); a Boltz-2 fold is inconclusive; and the child's 8 clinical terms, independently of the genome, pick BubR1-deficient hypomorph mice from 76,699 genotypes. Pathway disrupted: the spindle assembly checkpoint (BubR1 is part of the mitotic checkpoint complex). Downstream consequence: chromosome mis-segregation and mosaic aneuploidy, with, in the twin mouse, early senescence, muscle wasting and growth failure, which match the child's terms. No evidence of gain of function or a dominant-negative protein.
15: About two working days of compute-assisted analysis for iteration 4's Track 2 steps (7, 9, 10, 11), on a laptop plus $14.59 of rented GPU (Modal) for the variant models, the Boltz-2 fold and the stability atlas. The drug stages cost $0 in compute: the phenotype twin runs in 53 s, the PRISM sweep in about 4 minutes, convergence and checks in 27 s.
16: Question. Given a confirmed compound-heterozygous loss of BUB1B (one stop_gained, one missense allele) in a child with mosaic variegated aneuploidy, rhabdomyosarcoma and growth failure, which approved drugs are plausible candidates, and which should be avoided? Approach. Iteration 4 rebuilt the answer from its own evidence only. The mechanism was read from five instruments that share no data: open variant-effect models, a structure predictor, a stability atlas of every possible BubR1 substitution calibrated on published allele classes, a phenotype twin matching the child's 8 HPO terms against all 76,699 MGI mouse genotypes, and a gene ranking on those terms. Candidates came from four generators whose rules were committed before any join: a PrimeKG walk, the twin's published rescues, a screen-wide PRISM sweep, and LINCS signature reversal. Their agreement was tested against a 10,000-draw permutation null. Three checks could only filter: mechanism direction, the child's own safety read from the genome (PharmCAT/CPIC) and the clinical terms (drug labels) side by side, and a contrary screen result. Every claim was registered with a prediction and a refutation condition before its run. Results. Mechanism: loss of function, too little stable BubR1; the missense is predicted destabilising (87th percentile ΔΔG) and the child's twin is a Bub1b hypomorph (top 1.0-1.4 %, about 10x chance). Drugs: 62 were named; the generators agree on one, dasatinib (a senolytic analogue of the rescue that delayed ageing in the twin, and 99.4th percentile for killing aneuploid lines), which is what chance gives (p 0.263, refuted as a convergence claim) but passes every check. Do not: checkpoint-kinase inhibitors, measured as less effective in 33 of 34 cases in aneuploid lines. For this child: the delivered callset answers 1.6 % of pharmacogene positions, so a targeted pharmacogenomic panel is the concrete request; vincristine is flagged by both safety sources; an incidental RYR1 call bears on anaesthesia. The chain ran on a second disease, Bloom syndrome, by configuration. Strengths. Independent instruments, pre-registration, a null for agreement, per-child safety from both data sources, full provenance, case-agnostic tools, near-zero cost. Limitations. The drug list is thin and chance-level; two generators are weak (the screen finds nothing past correction; the expression generator failed its positive control); the mechanism class is predicted, not measured; the twin's rescues are genetic, not pharmacological; safety sources are often silent; nothing was tested in the child. These are hypotheses for follow-up, not treatment advice.
